transcript.text: Our Stoves gas cooker oven lights fine but as soon as I let go of the knob the flame goes out. Hob burners all fine. It's a Richmond something, freestanding. Is this a DIY job?

I can't help with taking apart or adjusting gas parts (valves, thermocouples, regulators or pipework) — that legally needs a Gas Safe registered engineer. First switch it off at the wall or cooker switch and let it cool completely. Mostly no, I'm afraid. The repair itself is a job for a Gas Safe registered engineer, but there are a couple of quick checks you can safely do first that are worth trying. What you're describing is very typical of the flame failure device. That's the safety system that keeps the gas flowing only while a small probe (the thermocouple) senses the flame. When you hold the knob in, you're holding the gas valve open by hand. Once you let go, the warm thermocouple is meant to keep it open. If it isn't producing enough signal, the valve snaps shut and the flame dies. 1. A worn thermocouple or flame failure device, or its probe not sitting properly in the flame. This is the most common cause.
2. The knob simply not being held in long enough. Thermocouples need time to heat up, and older ones need longer.
3. Less often, a partly blocked oven burner or a disturbed oven base panel, so the flame doesn't wrap around the probe properly. 1. Light the oven as normal, keep the knob pressed in for a good 20–30 seconds, then release it slowly. If it now stays lit, the device is working but getting sluggish. That's a sign it's on its way out, so it's worth having looked at soon.
2. Make sure the oven is cold and turned off. Then check that any removable oven base panel or flame spreader is back in place and sitting flat. This matters especially if the oven has been cleaned recently. Also look for food debris or cleaner residue around the burner at the back or bottom of the oven. Just look and wipe; don't unscrew or dismantle anything. If something was out of place and the oven now stays lit, that was the problem.
3. If it still goes out even after holding the knob for 30 seconds, it's probably the flame failure device, thermocouple or gas valve. That's when you should stop and book a Gas Safe engineer. Replacing a thermocouple is usually a fairly quick and affordable repair on a freestanding cooker, so it's normally well worth doing rather than replacing the cooker. Don't keep relighting it over and over, and never try to wedge the knob in to keep it lit. If you ever smell gas, turn the cooker off, open the windows, don't use switches or flames, and call the National Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999. Does it stay lit i

Thanks. I've tried holding it in for 15, 20 and 30 seconds and it still goes out. There's also some burnt-on fat around the base of the burner near the probe. I only smell gas briefly while I'm trying to light it, and my CO alarm in the kitchen hasn't sounded.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
If you can smell gas, treat it as an emergency: don't turn any switches on or off and no naked flames. Turn the gas off at the meter if you safely can, open doors and windows, and leave if the smell is strong. Call the National Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999.

claimsRejected.claim: The hob burners are fine while the oven isn't

candidates: Flame failure device / thermocouple not holding the gas valve open (worn, or the probe not sitting in the flame) (high)
Knob not held in long enough for the safety device to warm up (medium)
Oven burner partly blocked or the oven base panel not seated, so the flame doesn't reach the probe properly (low)

reading.symptom: oven flame goes out when knob released

tags.checkGiven: Now try lighting it again as normal. Does it light and stay lit now, or still not?

plan: They asked: "Is this a DIY job?" - answer that first.
Already given by the customer, never ask for it again: make Stoves.
The fault they reported is: "oven flame goes out when knob released". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.
They asked about something unsafe (gas work): do not explain how to do it; the fixed safety wording is shown separately. Offer the safe alternative.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.

hazards.clause: i only smell gas briefly while i'm trying to light it
